prompt: Discuss the tension between Aristotle's claim that phantasia always involves truth-apt representation and the possibility of deceptive or erroneous imagination.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis The tension between phantasia's truth-apt character and its susceptibility to deception emerges most sharply when one examines its relation to sense-perception, for Aristotle insists that imagination is commonly held to be a kind of movement that cannot occur without sensation, yet phantasia operates with a freedom that sensation itself does not enjoy. As Aristotle himself observes, "imagination takes place in the absence of both" faculty and activity—that is, in the absence of sight and seeing—"as e.g. in dreams" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 42). This claim establishes a fundamental contrast: whereas aisthesis is bound to the immediate presence of the sensible object and, at least with respect to its proper objects, achieves a kind of infallibility, phantasia retains the capacity to produce appearances even when the originating perceptual stimulus has withdrawn. Hawhee, drawing on the rhetorical dimensions of Aristotle's account, underscores phantasia's relationship to suasion and desire, noting that Aristotle describes it in connection with what "people long for on the basis of persuasion; for they desire to see and possess many things after hearing about" them (Hawhee 2011, p. [PAGE NEEDED]). Accordingly, the perceptual residue that phantasia preserves is not merely a passive trace but an active source of affective and deliberative power—one that can mislead precisely because it operates beyond the corrective reach of the present sensible object. Indeed, Papachristou leaves the term phantasia untranslated precisely because it resists reduction to "imagination" in any modern sense, noting that the Greek word encompasses a broader range of phenomena than its English counterpart would suggest (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). The internal distinction between sensory phantasia, shared by all animals, and deliberative phantasia, belonging only to calculative beings, will be addressed more fully below; here it suffices the gap between phantasia and aisthesis is the initial site where error becomes structurally possible. White the scholarly literature on De Anima III.3–8 has long struggled with the question of how imagination relates to truth, cataloguing debates about "imagination and truth in Aristotle" as central to any account of the faculty (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The relationship between phantasia as a capacity and the phantasma as its product introduces a further layer of complexity into the question of truth-aptness, for the phantasma is not simply a copy of a prior sensation but a representation that can be recombined, distorted, or voluntarily summoned. Aristotle distinguishes between "sensitive imagination," which "is found in all animals," and "deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). This passage reveals that the phantasma produced by deliberative phantasia is not merely a sensory remnant but an image shaped by comparative judgment—a feature that opens the faculty to both rational assessment and error, since the standard of measurement may itself be distorted by desire or habituation. Nussbaum critiques what she terms the "empiricist image theory," which holds that imagination always involves images that represent in virtue of similarity and that there are always two logically distinct processes—having an image and inspecting it (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 37). Against this reductive picture, Aristotle's own usage of phantasia remains closely linked to phainetai, the verb of appearing; thus "a man can be called 'false' if he often gives others a false impression, 'just as we call states of affairs false if they create a false phantasia'" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 37). The phantasma, accordingly, is not a neutral mental picture awaiting inspection but a mode of appearing that already carries evaluative and potentially deceptive significance. The voluntariness of phantasia—the fact that images can be summoned "at will," as Papachristou emphasizes—further complicates truth-aptness, for deliberate image-construction need not track perceptual fidelity (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 20–22). The relation of phantasma to doxa and belief will be elaborated in subsequent sections. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme Memory constitutes a domain in which phantasia's truth-apt structure is both presupposed and endangered, for recollection requires that the phantasma function as a reliable likeness of a prior perception, yet the very processes of temporal displacement and associative retrieval introduce the possibility of distortion. Nussbaum's account underscores that phantasia, even in apparently technical contexts, retains its connection to the language of appearing; thus "all men strive for the apparent good (phainomenon agathon): but no one is in control of the appearing (phantasia): the way the end appears (phainetai) to someone depends on what sort of a man he is" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 31–33). This passage, drawn from the Nicomachean Ethics, suggests that the phantasia operative in memory is not a neutral retrieval mechanism but one conditioned by character and habituation—hence its vulnerability to systematic error. White notes that the entanglement of imagination with truth has generated sustained scholarly debate, particularly regarding how phantasia mediates between sensation and intellection in contexts of recollection (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23). The temporal dimension is crucial: memory depends upon phantasmata that persist across time, yet this very persistence means that the original perceptual context has been lost, and the image must function as a sign of something absent. Heidegger's analysis of Aristotle's πάθη illuminates this structure, for affects are "not states pertaining to ensouled things, but are concerned with a disposition of living things in their world, in the mode of being positioned toward something, allowing a matter to matter to it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 96–98). Memory's phantasmata, accordingly, are shaped by the affective dispositions of the remembering subject, and the distinction between sensory and deliberative phantasia becomes relevant insofar as deliberative recall involves a comparative judgment that sensory memory does not require. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa The relationship between phantasia and doxa—belief or opinion—marks the point at which the question of deception becomes most acute, for while doxa is explicitly truth-apt and can be true or false, phantasia appears to operate with a representational character that is not straightforwardly propositional yet still carries evaluative force. Gonzalez, analyzing the function of phantasia in the Rhetoric, notes that opinion (doxa) is a rendering that men heed "only on account of those who hold it," suggesting that doxa depends upon the persuasive force of the speaker and the phantasia through which rhetorical demonstration is received (Gonzalez, *The Meaning and Function of Phantasia in Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' III.1*, pp. 14–15). O'Gorman "bringing before the eyes" is a lexical form of energeia, a type of motion realized through "the capacity of the mind for seeing objects in action," thereby linking phantasia's image-making power to the rhetorical formation of belief (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 5). Burke, for his part, notes that the term "imagination" itself risks being dismissed as "overly psychologistic and extraliterary in its origins," yet its operation in forming and deforming opinion cannot be dispensed with (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 97–99). The deceptive potential of phantasia thus lies precisely in its capacity to mediate between sensation and belief: because doxa frequently arises from how things appear (phainetai), and because phantasia governs the mode of that appearing, erroneous belief can result from phantasia's distortion of perceptual content. The internal distinction between sensory and deliberative grades of phantasia is essential here, for it is deliberative phantasia that produces the comparative images upon which practical doxa is formed—and it is in this deliberative register that the tension between truth-aptness and deception is most productively unresolved (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52).
